newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: West stymied from moving ahead with landmines ban.
newsitem.headline: West stymied from moving ahead with landmines ban.

text.p: Western countries, keen to start work on a global landmines ban, tried unsuccessfully on Thursday to bring any objectors out into the open.
Finland, supported in the U.N.-backed Conference on Disarmament by Australia, Britain, France and the United States, called on any members opposed to moving ahead on a ban to declare so publicly.
The request was designed to embarrass non-aligned states who have been accused of obstructing progress in the 61-member Conference.
Katharine Crittenberger, acting head of the U.S. delegation, took the floor to plead for other delegations to openly state their positions. "We would like to know where we stand," she said.
But after more than three hours of debate, Mexico objected to the Conference president formally putting the Finnish question -- effectively blocking the body from taking a consensus decision.

"We have a clear position. There is no consensus on the request for appointment of a special coordinator on mines," said Absa Claude Diallo, Senegal's ambassador who currently presides over the forum.
She said she would continue consultations on the question.
Finland, building on an Australian proposal of last month, had proposed that countries openly declare in Thursday's public session whether they objected to naming a special coordinator.

The idea was that the appointee should be asked to seek consensus on a mandate for launching negotiations to ban anti-personnel landmines, blamed for killing 25,000 people a year and maiming many more.
"We are going to try to see if we can get a decision on a special coordinator. If there is resistance we want it public and on the record," a Western diplomat said before debate began.
But he described the attitude of non-aligned countries in the Conference, who number about 26, as "obstreperous".
Western countries are keen to launch talks on landmines in the Geneva body, in parallel to Canada's "Ottawa Process" which aims to reach a ban among some 50 countries by the end of this year.
China and Russia -- major producers and users of landmines -- are not taking part in the Canadian bid. This means a viable, universal ban could only be clinched in Geneva, diplomats say.
But non-aligned countries say top priority should be given to concrete steps towards total nuclear disarmament, and only then would they be ready to work on issues including landmines.
Mexico, speaking on behalf of the non-aligned countries, on Thursday tabled the text of a mandate for a new committee to negotiate total nuclear disarmament within a specified time.

Brazil's envoy Gilberto Vergne Saboia supported the proposal, adding: "Nuclear disarmament is a legitimate aspiration of the international community. It is incumbent on the Conference on Disarmament to discharge its responsibility in this regard."
